strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in Electronic Design Automation (EDA)—estimating the quality (area and delay) of RTL designs early in the workflow, bypassing computationally intensive logic synthesis.

The proposed StructRTL framework uses Control Data Flow Graphs (CDFGs) rather than raw token sequences, allowing it to explicitly model the structural and control-data dependencies crucial for hardware timing and area properties.

The authors design domain-specific adaptations to standard graph self-supervised learning, such as masking post-GNN context-aware embeddings (instead of raw features) to avoid functional ambiguity, and using stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss to handle extreme class imbalances in CDFG node types.

The experimental evaluation is highly thorough, using a large dataset of 13,200 designs, comparing against strong recent LLM-based baselines (e.g., VeriDistill), and including robust evaluations of generalization across functionalities, design sizes, and real-world industrial designs.
The paper is very well-written, with clear explanations of the architecture and comprehensive ablation studies in the appendices.
weaknesses: The core machine learning techniques employed—such as the hybrid GNN-Transformer architecture, Laplacian positional encodings, masked node feature reconstruction (reminiscent of GraphMAE), and link prediction—are largely adapted from existing graph neural network literature, representing a somewhat incremental methodological novelty.

The knowledge distillation (KD) phase requires first synthesizing and mapping RTL designs to post-mapping (PM) netlists to train the teacher model. While this is only done during training (with inference remaining fast), the dependency on running a full industrial synthesis toolchain (Yosys + ABC) to generate the training data is still high.

strengths: Well-motivated methodology: The authors identify a crucial limitation in applying standard Graph Masked Autoencoders to hardware graphs (the ambiguity of masking strict functional operators) and resolve it elegantly by masking post-GNN context-aware embeddings instead of raw node features.

Comprehensive and robust training designs: To tackle the extreme class imbalance inherent in circuit graph node types (where wires dominate over operators), the paper successfully integrates stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss.
Rigorous evaluation on a large dataset: Evaluating on over 13,200 designs is a significant improvement over classic EDA ML papers that often evaluate on fewer than 100 designs.

Effective cross-stage knowledge distillation: The integration of a post-mapping netlist (gate-level) teacher model to guide the RTL-level predictor bridges the gap between RTL and post-synthesis stages, leading to substantial performance boosts.

Practical industrial verification: The inclusion of evaluations on 51 industrial design pairs (with more than 10,000 nodes each) and a pilot study on register-boundary partitioning demonstrates the practical utility and scalability of the proposed method.
weaknesses: Dependency on parsing infrastructure: The extraction of CDFGs relies heavily on Yosys compiling RTL into RTLIL and a specific Verilog parser. Complex SystemVerilog constructs or non-synthesizable testbench code might cause failures in CDFG generation, which is a potential bottleneck.

Performance gap on sequential circuits: As shown in the experiments, there remains a noticeable performance gap on sequential circuits compared to combinational ones due to intricate inter-cycle dependencies, which are not yet fully captured by the current pretraining objectives.

Focus on relative ranking over absolute accuracy: The target variables are log-transformed, which aligns well with ranking tasks but may limit applicability when absolute physical constraint violations (e.g., strict maximum delay limits) must be predicted with high precision.

strengths: Comprehensive and Sound Methodology: The paper presents StructRTL, which elegantly combines a GIN with a Transformer encoder and global positional encodings (Laplacian eigenvectors) to process control data flow graphs (CDFGs).

Novel Self-Supervised Objectives: Proposes masking post-GNN context-aware embeddings rather than raw features, which avoids functional ambiguity in computational graphs. Incorporates stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss to address severe node type imbalance.

Cross-Stage Supervision via Knowledge Distillation: Successfully transfers fine-grained, low-level physical insights from post-mapping netlists (the teacher model) to the high-level CDFG representation (the student), leading to massive performance gains.

Thorough and Rigorous Evaluation: Evaluates on a large dataset of 13,200 designs, comparing against both classical graph baselines and state-of-the-art Verilog LLMs. Includes comprehensive out-of-distribution, functional, size-based generalization tests, and validation on real-world industrial design pairs.

Excellent Practical Focus: Analyzes inference latency (offering a 145x speedup over synthesis), scaling with graph size, and provides a pilot study on register-boundary partitioning for handling very large designs.
weaknesses: Baseline LLM Configuration: The comparison with LLMs uses frozen backbones. While the authors demonstrate that full fine-tuning of a 7B LLM on the target dataset leads to severe overfitting (Table 11), a modern parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approach (such as LoRA) could have been evaluated as a more competitive LLM-based baseline.

Clarity on Pretraining Dataset: It is not entirely clear whether the self-supervised pretraining was conducted on the exact same 13,200 designs (acting as a joint-training/unsupervised regularization stage) or on a larger, separate unlabeled dataset. Clarifying this would help assess the framework's data requirements.

Technology Node Dependency: The knowledge distillation and synthesis flow are tied to the SkyWater 130nm library. While the authors discuss technology node migration as a limitation, demonstrating how easily the model adapts to a different technology node (e.g., 45nm or 7nm) using the proposed limited-data adaptation strategy would make the evaluation much more robust.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and important problem in EDA: estimating post-synthesis quality metrics (area and delay) directly from RTL, which significantly speeds up the design loop.
The proposed framework, StructRTL, is well-designed. It combines GNNs with a Transformer encoder using Laplacian positional embeddings, which effectively models the structural semantics of CDFGs.

The pretraining tasks (masked node modeling and edge prediction) are tailored for CDFGs by applying masking on the post-GNN embedding space and incorporating stratified masking with class-balanced focal loss to handle severe class imbalance.
The incorporation of cross-stage knowledge distillation from post-mapping netlist representations is an effective way to bridge the abstraction gap between RTL and gate-level designs.
Empirical evaluations show significant improvements over both traditional graph methods and large-scale LLM baselines (such as 7B parameter CodeV models) in predicting area and delay.
weaknesses: The dataset consists of relatively small designs; Table 3 shows that over 80% of the designs (10,645 out of 13,200) have fewer than 600 nodes in their CDFGs. Real-world industrial RTL designs are orders of magnitude larger, and the paper lacks evaluation or discussion on how the model scales to complex, large-scale designs.

The technical novelty is somewhat limited as it combines several existing concepts (GraphMAE, MaskGAE, Laplacian positional encodings, and knowledge distillation) without major theoretical departures.

The CDFG construction relies on a multi-step parsing pipeline (Yosys -> RTLIL -> Stagira parser -> AST -> CDFG). Academic Verilog/SystemVerilog parsers often suffer from limited support for modern language constructs. The robustness of this parsing pipeline on complex, commercial-grade RTL is not evaluated or discussed.

The paper lacks an analysis of the computational overhead and runtime. Since the goal is to provide fast feedback compared to the synthesis toolchain, a comparative runtime analysis (e.g., inference time vs. Yosys+ABC logic synthesis time) would help quantify the actual productivity gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and critical bottleneck in Electronic Design Automation (EDA)—rapid and accurate estimation of post-synthesis quality metrics (area and delay) directly from Register Transfer Level (RTL) code.

Using a Control Data Flow Graph (CDFG) representation allows the model to explicitly capture structural and computational semantics, successfully demonstrating that structural representations can outperform token-based Large Language Models (LLMs) on topology-sensitive physical prediction tasks.

The self-supervised learning strategy is carefully adapted for CDFGs, specifically employing post-GNN context-aware embedding masking, stratified masking, and class-balanced focal loss to effectively handle the severe class imbalance of operator versus wire/register nodes.

The cross-stage knowledge distillation framework is well-conceived, effectively transferring low-level gate-level insights from a Post-Mapping (PM) netlist predictor into the RTL-stage CDFG predictor during training.
Evaluation on a large-scale dataset of 13,200 designs shows substantial improvements over both graph-based and powerful LLM-based baselines (such as CodeV).
weaknesses: The architectural components (combining GIN, Laplacian positional embeddings, and Transformers) are largely drawn from established Graph Transformer frameworks (e.g., GraphGPS). The conceptual novelty lies more in the domain adaptation and specialized SSL tasks rather than fundamental graph learning theory.

The dataset splitting strategy uses an 80:20 split for training and validation, but does not mention a separate, held-out test set. Evaluation on the validation set can introduce optimistic bias if any hyperparameter tuning or early stopping was performed based on validation metrics.

The majority of designs in the dataset are relatively small (fewer than 600 nodes, as shown in Table 3). Real-world industrial designs are often orders of magnitude larger. The paper lacks discussion or evaluation regarding the model's scalability and generalization to larger-scale designs.

The CDFG generation pipeline depends on Yosys and the Stagira Verilog parser. The robustness of this front-end parser to complex SystemVerilog constructs, third-party IP blocks, and parameterized modules is not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and highly practical problem in Electronic Design Automation (EDA)—accelerating RTL design iterations by estimating post-synthesis quality metrics (area and delay) directly from RTL.

The proposed StructRTL framework shifts from token-based views to structural graph (CDFG) views, capturing circuit topology and control/data flow semantics much more naturally than sequence-based models.

The pretraining methodology is well-designed; applying masking at the post-GNN embedding layer instead of raw features prevents semantic ambiguity, while stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss effectively handle the severe class imbalance of operator nodes.

The integration of cross-stage knowledge distillation (KD) from a post-mapping (PM) netlist predictor is highly effective at injecting gate-level physical implementation details into the high-level CDFG predictor.
The experiments are extensive and show clear improvements over state-of-the-art LLM-based and graph-based baselines, verified on a large dataset of over 13,000 designs with thorough ablation studies.
weaknesses: The dataset is composed of relatively small-to-medium scale designs (mostly under 600 nodes in CDFGs, as indicated in Figure 4 and Table 3). The paper lacks a discussion or evaluation of how the proposed GNN-Transformer architecture scales to massive, complex industrial RTL designs.

The methodology is heavily dependent on the specific logic synthesis and technology library (Yosys, ABC, SkyWater 130nm) used to train the teacher (PM predictor). The authors do not explore how the learned representations transfer or adapt when synthesis constraints, tools, or target cell libraries change.

There is no detailed profiling of the computational overhead (inference time and memory usage) of StructRTL compared to the baselines. Although it is faster than full logic synthesis, understanding the latency of GNN+Transformer-based estimation on massive graphs is important.
